CausalChain: Tumor cells exhibit high glycolytic activity -> Increased lactate secretion into TME -> Uptake of lactate by MDSCs -> Lactate induces histone lactylation in MDSCs (synergizing with GM‑CSF/STAT3 signaling) -> Upregulation of immunosuppressive genes (e.g., ARG1, iNOS) -> Enhanced T cell suppression and immune evasion -> Tumor progression
Hypothesis: Tumor-derived lactate, a byproduct of the enhanced glycolytic activity of tumor cells, is taken up by MDSCs and induces histone lactylation, thereby shifting these cells toward a potent immunosuppressive state. This lactate-mediated epigenetic reprogramming acts in parallel with well-established pro-tumorigenic signals (e.g., GM‑CSF/STAT3) to upregulate key immunosuppressive genes, such as ARG1 and iNOS, which inhibit T cell activity and promote tumor immune evasion. We hypothesize that therapeutic strategies which combine inhibition of lactate production or blockade of lactate transport/lactylation (using specific inhibitors or CRISPR-mediated disruption of lactylation enzymes) with targeting of the GM‑CSF/STAT3 axis will significantly impair MDSC function, reduce tumor progression, and enhance the efficacy of cancer immunotherapies. Contemporary techniques like single-cell RNA sequencing and high-resolution epigenomic profiling will be pivotal in validating each step of this causal chain.
Abstract: We propose that tumor cells, characterized by high glycolytic activity, secrete lactate which is subsequently transported into myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Within these immunosuppressive cells, lactate acts not only as a metabolic byproduct but also as a signaling molecule that induces histone lactylation. This epigenetic modification, in concert with established pro‐inflammatory signals such as GM‑CSF/STAT3, upregulates immunosuppressive genes (e.g., ARG1, iNOS), thereby potentiating T cell suppression and promoting tumor progression. Leveraging cutting‐edge technologies—including single‐cell transcriptomics, CRISPR‐based genetic screens, and high‐resolution epigenomic mapping (e.g., CUT&RUN and ChIP‐seq)—this hypothesis aims to dissect the multifaceted role of lactate in reprogramming MDSCs. Furthermore, we posit that combinatorial therapeutic strategies targeting lactate production, lactate transport, or specific lactylation enzymes, alongside inhibition of parallel signaling pathways such as GM‑CSF/STAT3, may disrupt this immunosuppressive circuit and enhance the efficacy of cancer immunotherapies.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that tumor-derived lactate promotes histone lactylation in MDSCs, thereby enhancing their immunosuppressive function and contributing to tumor progression, with a concomitant suggestion that targeting lactate production or lactylation could alleviate immunosuppression. The revised hypothesis builds on this foundation by explicitly incorporating the established role of GM‑CSF/STAT3 signaling in MDSC activation as a synergistic factor alongside lactate-induced histone lactylation. Each causal step from tumor glycolysis to immune evasion is explicitly maintained: (1) high glycolytic activity leads to increased lactate secretion, (2) lactate is taken up by MDSCs, (3) lactate induces histone lactylation (now acknowledged to possibly work in tandem with GM‐CSF/STAT3 signaling), (4) this modification upregulates immunosuppressive genes, and (5) the resultant MDSC activity facilitates T cell suppression and tumor progression. Additionally, the revised hypothesis leverages modern technological advances to improve experimental validation and therapeutic targeting, thus enhancing its practical implementability and translational potential.
